460.t: The Afro-Classic album and Amazing Grace: fathers' reactions
460.s: Brown shows his copy of Afro-Classic and tells how his father responded to Amazing Grace. Laws says his own father cried on hearing it.
460.ch: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
460.q: Wow, that’s interesting. My dad too, but he only related to Amazing Grace. He cried when he heard that. Tears came to his eyes. That was significant for me.

460.t: His parents' reaction and Amazing Grace for his father
460.s: Laws says his mother supported him while his deacon father thought jazz was the devil's music until the money came in. His father's humming of Amazing Grace led Laws to record it on Morning Star.
460.q: She was a supporter. She’s always a supporter. She didn’t – she felt my dad was too restrictive. Of course the only thing my dad ever understood about any music I played was one piece. I recorded it for him, and that still became – as a matter of fact, at that NEA award, they had on our tables what…

67.t: How his family finally accepted his jazz career
67.s: His parents accepted it once they saw he took care of himself, sent them money, and did not become a drunk.
67.q: -- as soon as they found out -- learned that I was taking care of myself. That was their main worry. They knew I was taking care of myself and I was keeping in touch with them all the time. I'd go to see them all the time. Send money every week to my mother, send things to my father. Clothes, and…

67.t: Family's worry about music as a career
67.s: His doctor relatives did not object, but his father feared musicians drank and wanted him in medical school; jazz was seen as low down and sinful.
67.q: Well, they didn't -- they didn't object. None of them objected. My father, he -- he was kind of -- little worried about it because in those days, musicians would the in Nashville he was see that -- natural, there wasn't too much going on like a street band, military band and that --

846.t: What families thought of jazz and of a musician's career
846.s: With no radio, families welcomed home music, but a career as a jazz musician was thought damnable.
846.ch: Society bands and white New Orleans attitudes
846.q: Well, for one thing you must remember, that there was no radio or television at all. The movies were silent movies. And we had to afford a great deal of our own entertainment, which came through the string instrument. And the families were always for that because it kept us together and they knew…

15.t: Parents' reaction; a family of entertainers
15.s: His mother came to Milwaukee after the first pay; two band members knew his father, and his parents were singers and dancers in vaudeville.
15.q: Well, my mother knew where I was first week. I wanted to write and they wouldn't let me. So when I got my first pay, they didn't take nothing out, see. Make a big impression, send a full week's salary home. And my mother was up there that afternoon. Milwaukee was only 85 miles and so on. Yes, yeah.…

535.s: His parents neither encouraged nor discouraged him, and his uncle saw him only on TV and records.
535.ch: New York and the Brubeck years
535.q: No. But they didn’t tell me not to. They didn’t say yeah man, keep practicing you know. They just went, “This guy’s nuts look at him. What’s he —” that sort of thing. They just left me alone which is good enough.

791.s: Her parents found her path a mystery but were happy she did what she wanted.
791.q: Well you know I think I was kind of a mystery to them, what it was that I was doing. But you know I’m sure they were happy that I was doing what I wanted to do. That was probably the most important thing to them. They didn’t entirely understand it but you know that’s the way it goes.

914.t: His father's reaction to his name on a television scroll
914.s: His father, who hated jazz, watched his first show and said it was too bad it took so long.
914.q: It felt great. Warren was talking about his parents. My parents were not quite the same way. I remember I went down to where my parents were living at the time and I put on this station and I played this show. My parents never — my father would play classical music. He hated jazz. He hated my…

394.t: Her father's and mother's reactions to her music
394.s: Her father dislikes what she plays, perhaps from his own unrealized rock and roll ambitions; her mother, a writer and poet, supports her and performed with her.
394.q: I’ve got two answers for you. The first one is not really. My dad doesn’t like – well he likes a bit of trad jazz and he doesn’t like what I do even though he values the fact that I do something which requires a certain amount of skill and discipline. And I think there’s also an element of jealousy…

322.t: His parents' attitude and his father's gift of gab
322.s: His mother accepted music as a career; his father was a musician out of necessity and a great talker.
322.q: Oh I don’t think my mother — she was all right with it. My father had no interest in being a musician. He was a musician out of necessity you know, to make money. But he was more of an organizer, more of a leader of men. He had the greatest gift of gab of anybody that I’ve ever met on this planet…

107.s: His parents supported him and bought his instruments; his father's 'bippity bop' remark shows new music is not meant for the older generation.
107.q: Yes they were. They were always supportive. They always encouraged me to practice, to work hard. They bought every instrument that I owned until I was 21.

835.s: Humphrey says his parents have always supported what he does.
835.q: I don’t know. I never asked him. He never told me. I don’t think my mother is surprised, and probably my father isn’t either. You know what I mean? He supports everything I do. They’ve always supported everything I do, and I’m thankful for that. They didn’t try to steer me some other way.

996.t: Parents' attitude and their disrupted wartime schooling
996.s: His parents accepted guitar if he had a fallback; his father wanted him on tenor sax and gave him recorders.
996.q: I mean they were fine with me playing the guitar, from their point of view, as long as I had something to fall back on. And I was never academic enough to go for medicine, which would have been kind of the brass ring, to be a doctor. So I said well maybe a pharmacist. But the thing is both of my…

998.s: Her parents' support for setting goals and what she wanted from the Ray Brown lesson.
998.q: Well it’s just one of those things — my mother and father have always been really supportive about setting goals. You see something that you want, and you take the steps that it takes to get there. And it means practicing, it means self-sacrifice, it means you do the stuff that needs to be done.…

337.t: His father's later support and opera
337.s: His father only heard him near the end, his mother was his supporter, and his father loved opera.
337.q: Near the end. I did a couple of concerts at the library and so on, and he saw it. But my mother was really my greatest supporter, she was the one. But my father was mad at me all this time, until his death bed, which was amazing.

793.t: Classical grandparents who supported her jazz
793.s: Her classical-musician grandparents worried about jazz but respected her seriousness and supported her; she and Rowe talk about 'getting' music.
793.q: Yes. My grandfather said to me once, you know, “I worry about you playing this jazz music” you know, “there are drugs and alcohol” and you know, “why don’t you get a job like in a symphony or something?” And I told him that this is the music I really love. And they were both very broad-minded and…

697.t: His father wanted him to be a minister
697.s: His father hoped he would be a minister, and later told him he had become one through his music.
697.q: Well I tried. My father wanted me to be a minister. And I wanted to be a musician. And it was very meaningful that years and years later my dad went to a concert in Italy where I was playing with Gerry and at the end of the concert he said, “I always wanted you to be a minister and you became one…

361.t: Family reactions to a jazz career
361.s: His doctor brothers, his father's taste for Frankie Carle, and jazz as specialized music.
361.q: It’s a specialized kind of a thing. I think we all have to admit that jazz isn’t a front runner as far as public knowledge. Everybody doesn’t know about jazz music, because like what you said, it’s a very select kind of a thing. But anyway I thought that was a funny thing. But anyway little by…

362.t: His strict father and the family's reaction to jazz
362.s: His father wanted university and a job; after his mother died when Tanaka was 17 he softened.
362.q: My father is a very strict person, you know, very down to earth. And you had to go to the university and find a job. My mother — my father always kind of had the upper hand. So I must follow whatever my father — my mother passed away when I was 17 years old. At that time my father’s friend said to…

85.t: Parents' views of jazz and the saxophone
85.s: His churchgoing parents considered jazz the devil's music and wanted him to be a violinist or theologian.
85.q: Well, no. They thought it was, you know, undignified and demeaning to the black race. At that particular time, I think they even called it “devil’s music,” you know, “music of the devil.” Of course, my parents, being churchgoing and God-fearing, they really did not care for the music. My sister,…

225.t: Cousins' and relatives' reactions to his career choice
225.s: No relatives were musicians; some considered him odd for becoming one.
225.q: None of my cousins or relatives in that area were in music or the arts or entertainment whatsoever. I was the oddball, I guess you might say. I think some of them considered me to be a little bit odd. Some of them accepted [it] as being, well, that’s what he wants to do and I wish him well. Others…

508.t: Buying Earth, Wind and Fire's record and his father's reaction to Maurice White
508.s: His father recognizes Maurice White, once a drummer in Ramsey Lewis's band, and is simply happy for his friend's success, a model for Branford.
508.q: Right. Check you out. But the first one I bought was Open Our Eyes. I said, “Man there’s this band. You gotta hear it.” You know, where it was mostly for “Mighty Mighty.” That was the song that was on the radio. So I bought it. And my dad…. “May I see the record?” And my dad burst out laughing, he…

1.t: Grandmother says jazz is the Devil's music
1.s: His paternal grandmother disapproved of jazz and had never seen a movie.
1.ch: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
1.q: My grandma said, "Jazz music is nothin' but the Devil's music, because it entices people to live a fast life. Danny, that's not no life," she told me when I first started... "Son, you're going to be a Jazz...play that music? That ain't no way to make no honest living." My grandmother, Miss Barker,…

377.s: Basie says his mother approved of most things he wanted to do and his father did not discourage him; the interviewer starts on the Blue Devils.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Oh, yeah. (Inaudible). So did my daddy. He was pretty well -- I guess he seen me with (inaudible) you make me turn another way; he probably wanted me (inaudible) know? Just trying to (inaudible) didn't discourage me.

614.t: Parents' doubts about a musician's career and music in the household
614.s: His parents lost enthusiasm when he chose to be a musician rather than a performer, until he became a bandleader. His father had good taste and a player-piano with classical rolls.
614.q: Well, actually, the support was beginning to run thin at the point when I had definitely made up my mind I was going to be a musician and not a performer.

378.t: Second brother's low opinion of musicians
378.s: The brother in Oklahoma thought musicians were drunkards and dope fiends, objected to his leaving school and never forgave the change of name.
378.q: Except that the one in Oklahoma, never gave -- never -- never liked the idea of me becoming a musician. You know. Oh, they were so against it.

381.t: Cousin Harold Newchurch and house-party musicians
381.s: His trumpet-playing cousin Harold played Miami house parties for drinks, which left his father convinced musicians were worthless.
381.q: Well, I had a cousin of mine who was a trumpet player -- my cousin Harold, Harold Newchurch, and he used to play all the house parties around Miami.

454.t: Duke on avant-garde records, and Ornette's confident upbringing
454.s: Ellington declines to go back to avant-garde; Mingus contrasts Ornette's parented confidence with his own struggle for approval.
454.ch: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
454.q: Red Norvo said one good thing in his life. When he first heard some kids playing, he said, it reminds me of some kids, you give them some blocks, and Mama says he can do anything he wants to do with them, stack them up this way and that way, and they say, look, Mommy, what I've done.

428.t: Hall's parents and their attitude to his music
428.s: His parents' work and their payment for lessons without any other involvement.
428.q: Yes. My mother was Alene K. Hall. It's funny that her middle initial was K, because my nickname has been Al Kay Hall (inaudible), and mine is W. (Laughter.) And my father's Henry.
